_comment: A learned generator on the same dependence benchmark, and why the training budget
turned out to be the finding.
Synthea and carebundle are both rule-based, so a shared blind spot between them
would say nothing about generators in general. CTGAN trained on individual NHANES
rows is the strongest available test: it has the most direct possible access to the
dependence structure of any generator here.
Access is deliberately unequal and that must be stated when quoting these:
carebundle   fitted to NHANES aggregates (quantiles, correlations)
CTGAN        trained on individual NHANES rows

task._note: Train/test split so no generator is scored against rows it was fitted on.

ctgan_3000_epochs_full_data._caveat: Trained on all 1213 rows including the evaluation half. An optimistic bound, not a fair score. Included to separate 'needs more data' from 'loses structure' — it is barely better than the fair 3000-epoch run, so the answer is training budget, not sample size.

finding: A first run at 300 epochs gave 0.191 mean deviation and 8/12 sign agreement, which
reads as 'a learned model loses cross-domain dependence'. That was wrong, and it was
an under-training artefact. At 3000 epochs CTGAN reaches 0.074 and 12/12 — comparable
to carebundle and far better than Synthea's 0.208.
What survives is more useful than the claim it replaced. The dependence ratio climbs
0.99 -> 1.05 -> 1.59 across training budgets against a true 1.76: CTGAN produces
essentially INDEPENDENT analytes until somewhere past 1000 epochs, then acquires the
joint structure. And the co-occurrence rate swings 36.7% -> 9.1% -> 14.5% against a
stable truth of 15.0% — a four-fold swing driven purely by a hyperparameter.
The practical warning: a marginal check cannot tell you whether a GAN has converged
on the joint distribution. At 300 epochs the ratio is 0.99, meaning the analytes are
independent, while the headline co-occurrence rate is more than twice reality. Both
numbers are wrong for opposite reasons and neither is visible without the
caveats: 606 training rows is small for a GAN; the full-data run bounds how much that costs.
CPU-only training; no hyperparameter search beyond the epoch sweep.
Two architectures, both from the ctgan package. No diffusion or copula-based model tested.

The dependence measure scores whatever pairs a source carries: CTGAN and TVAE supply four analytes and so are scored over 8 cells, against 14 for a FHIR source that also emits weight and HbA1c. The sign column shows the count; the deviations are not over identical pair sets.
cross_architecture: TVAE was added because one model's behaviour is not a property of learned
generators. It optimises a different objective from a GAN, so a failure appearing in
both is about the class rather than about adversarial training.
Both converge by 3000 epochs and both are badly wrong before it — in OPPOSITE
directions. CTGAN drifts toward independence (ratio 0.99 at 300 epochs, against a
true 1.76). TVAE over-couples (2.36). Neither error is in the same place, and a
practitioner tuning one would learn nothing about the other.
The detail that matters most: **TVAE held 12/12 sign agreement at every epoch count**
while its co-occurrence rate was 2.0% against a true 15.0%. Sign agreement — the
obvious sanity check on a correlation table — was completely uninformative. So was

residual_bias_at_3000_epochs.ctgan: P(>=3) 14.5% against 15.0% — nearly exact — but ratio 1.59 against 1.76, so slightly under-clustered with marginals a little too abnormal.
residual_bias_at_3000_epochs.tvae: ratio 1.80 against 1.76 — nearly exact — but P(>=3) 10.6% against 15.0%, so correctly clustered with marginals too mild.
residual_bias_at_3000_epochs._note: The two converge to different residual biases. Reporting either metric alone would rank them differently, which is an argument for reporting both.
